one_liner: FAIR's all-C++ end-to-end speech-recognition training toolkit; its 2018 paper claims faster training than ESPnet, Kaldi and OpenSeq2Seq.
what_it_does: A complete acoustic-model training and decoding pipeline written in C++: Train, Test and Decode executables driven by gflags flag files and text architecture files, with CTC, ASG (auto-segmentation), seq2seq and transformer criteria, MFCC/MFSC featurization and a lexicon or lexicon-free beam-search decoder with KenLM language models. The v0.2 release also ships Python bindings for the ASG criterion, featurization and decoder, and the wav2letter@anywhere streaming inference platform (FBGEMM backend). The main branch now holds only paper recipes, pretrained models and data preparation, built against Flashlight 0.3's ASR app; you adopt its whole training pipeline rather than swapping it into an ESPnet, Kaldi or OpenSeq2Seq setup.
how_it_is_fast: There is no Python interpreter in the training loop: models run on Flashlight's tape autograd over ArrayFire tensors (per the catalogued Flashlight entry, ArrayFire JIT-fuses element-wise ops and convolutions and RNNs go to cuDNN), and multi-GPU training is synchronous data-parallel through Flashlight's distributed backend, which the build requires. The ASG loss has hand-written CUDA kernels (one thread block per batch item and token per time step, CUB BlockReduce max and sum for a log-sum-exp forward/backward recursion, double-precision accumulators in a single preallocated workspace), CTC on GPU goes through the vendored Baidu warp-ctc, and feature loading is prefetched on a thread pool (--nthread futures cache). Decoding is a C++ beam search over a lexicon trie with a per-frame token beam (top-K partial sort), score-threshold pruning, hypothesis merging by sort plus optional log-add, and an LM-state cache.
when_to_use: Reproducing FAIR's 2016-2020 ASR papers and pretrained models (conv_glu, seq2seq_tds, lexicon_free, sota/2019, streaming_convnets, self_training, slimIPL, MLS) exactly; the README says this requires Flashlight <= 0.3.2.
Training CTC or ASG acoustic models from a pure C++ stack on Linux with NVIDIA GPUs and MPI-based multi-node data parallelism, with no Python runtime.
Reusing the ASG criterion kernels (CUDA and CPU) or the KenLM-backed lexicon beam-search decoder on their own, via v0.2's libraries-only build (W2L_BUILD_LIBRARIES_ONLY) or its Python bindings.
As a reference for how a 2018 C++ ASR system organised its loss kernels, decoder pruning and prefetching data loader.
when_not_to_use: New ASR projects: the README says development moved to Flashlight's ASR application, and every commit since 2023 is a Meta-internal lint, formatter or build sync; v0.2 is tied to Flashlight v0.2 and ArrayFire >= 3.6.1, and main refuses to configure against Flashlight >= 0.4.
Expecting the speed claim to hold today: the only comparison is against 2018 versions of ESPnet, Kaldi and OpenSeq2Seq, and no comparison with any current toolkit was found.

ASG with large output vocabularies: the CUDA ASG workspace holds two B x N x N double-precision buffers plus two B x T x N ones, so memory grows quadratically with the token set; issue #802 reports a 12.8 GB allocation failure on a V100 after switching a working CTC setup to ASG.

Teams without time to tune: users report slow training (issue #621 conv_glu on a P40 at 2.10 sec/sec, #835 4x T4 at 67.79 sec/sec and 18 h per epoch on about 1,000 h of audio, #672 a Transformer on 1k h LibriSpeech taking over a week on one GPU) with no maintainer diagnosis visible.
Non-Ubuntu or non-NVIDIA setups: the tested paths are the CPU and CUDA Dockerfiles; issue #800 is titled 'Cannot build wav2letter on non-ubuntu systems', and macOS and Windows are not documented.

integration.form: CMake project building executables (Train, Test, Decode) and static libraries (wav2letter-libraries, with a libraries-only option); main builds only recipe tools against an installed Flashlight 0.3
integration.dependencies: v0.2: Flashlight v0.2 built with distributed and contrib targets, ArrayFire >= 3.6.1, KenLM, gflags, glog, FFTW3, libsndfile, a BLAS (ATLAS, OpenBLAS, Accelerate or MKL), optional OpenMP; on GPU CUDA >= 9.2 with vendored warp-ctc and auto-downloaded CUB 1.8.0; inference platform: FBGEMM and cereal. main: Flashlight 0.3.x (< 0.4) built with app/asr (flashlight::fl_pkg_speech)
integration.min_toolchain: v0.2: C++11, g++ >= 4.8, CMake >= 3.5.1, CUDA >= 9.2. main recipes: C++17 and CMake 3.10 (a stale CMakeLists comment says C++14)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with NVIDIA CUDA GPUs (main path) or Flashlight's CPU backend; Dockerfiles for CPU, CUDA and inference; other platforms not documented
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the libraries; W2lDataset::get() is marked thread-hostile when --nthread > 0 (one caller thread, sequential indices)

gotchas: No benchmark harness to check: neither the v0.2 tree nor main contains scripts or configs for the ESPnet/Kaldi/OpenSeq2Seq comparison, and an issue search for 'benchmark speed' returns nothing, so the paper's per-framework times cannot be reproduced from the repository.

The CUDA CTC criterion (src/criterion/backend/cuda/ConnectionistTemporalClassificationCriterion.cpp, v0.2) passes an input length of T for every utterance, so padding frames are scored as speech, and silently clips each target so that length plus repeats fits in T ('A heuristic to modify target length'), truncating over-long transcripts without a warning; it also copies targets, target sizes and scales to the host on every batch.
ASG kernels accumulate in double precision and preallocate B x T x N and B x N x N double buffers per call (FullConnectionCriterion.cu), which is what makes ASG memory-hungry for big token sets.
Licence labels disagree: the main README and GitHub's sidebar say MIT, but the LICENSE file (and the v0.2 README) carry the BSD licence text for wav2letter++; both are permissive.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over Flashlight, its catalogued successor that absorbed this code as the ASR app, only to reproduce the pre-2021 wav2letter recipes and models on a pinned Flashlight <= 0.3.2 or v0.2 stack; for new C++ training use Flashlight, and for Python-first work PyTorch.
verified_claims_summary: First-party FAIR paper (arXiv 1812.07625, ICASSP 2019), seen only through search-result summaries: on WSJ with 4 utterances per GPU on machines with eight 16 GB V100s, wav2letter++ trained a 30M-parameter DeepSpeech-2-style RNN (2 conv, 5 BiLSTM, 2 linear layers) more than 15% faster than the next-best of ESPnet, Kaldi and OpenSeq2Seq (fp32 and mixed-precision fp16 runs) even on one GPU, was 'in some cases more than 2x faster', and scaled linearly to 64 GPUs on a 100M-parameter model of 18 temporal convolutions plus 1 linear layer. Framework versions, compiler flags, CPU model and the per-framework times per batch were not seen.
status_note: Effectively abandoned since the 2020-21 move into Flashlight (latest commit 2026-08-28 is an automated lint fix, 98 open issues) but BSD-licensed and usable as a reference or for recipe reproduction on a pinned Flashlight <= 0.3.2 or v0.2 stack; the speed claim rests on a first-party 2018 paper read through snippets only.
sources_read: WebSearch snippets for arXiv 1812.07625 (arxiv.org, deepai.org and hgpu.org were EGRESS_BLOCKED)
